title: The Top Idea in Your Mind
author: Paul Graham
summary: Paul Graham argues that most people hold one "top idea" in their mind, the thought their attention drifts toward when allowed to wander, such as in the morning shower. Because hard problems are solved by this kind of ambient thinking, the top idea gets all of its benefit while everything else is starved. He says it is a disaster to let the wrong idea take that position, and illustrates it with startups that stall once they begin raising money. Money and disputes are the two especially sticky attention sinks, and he cites Newton's years lost to disputes over his theory of colors. Since thoughts cannot be controlled directly, the practical lesson is to control the situations you let yourself get into, and to forgive injuries partly out of selfish interest in protecting your attention.
points: Most people have one top idea that their mind returns to when it drifts, and it receives the benefit of unforced, background thinking.
Raising money is an attention sink because it has to be the thing you think about, which is why startups get little else done while fundraising.
Disputes are the second major trap because they feel as engaging as real ideas but have no substance behind them.
You cannot steer your thoughts directly, but you can steer them indirectly by choosing which situations become critical to you.
A simple test for your own top idea is to notice what your thoughts keep returning to in the shower, and to change something if it is the wrong thing.
quotes: I think most people have one top idea in their mind at any given time.

The problem is that once you start raising money, raising money becomes the top idea in your mind.
You can't directly control where your thoughts drift. If you're controlling them, they're not drifting. But you can control them indirectly, by controlling what situations you let yourself get into.
These too are engaging in the wrong way: they have the same velcro-like shape as genuinely interesting ideas, but without the substance.
Someone who does you an injury hurts you twice: first by the injury itself, and second by taking up your time afterward thinking about it.
But it's easy to figure this out: just take a shower. What topic do your thoughts keep returning to?
